summary.text: Define the candidate sequence by \(b_{n+3}=4b_{n+2}-b_n\) with the three required initial values, and set \(r_n=b_{n+1}^2-b_nb_{n+2}\). Induction gives a positive recurrence for \(r_n\) together with \(0<r_n\le b_n\), so \(b_{n+1}^2=b_nb_{n+2}+r_n\) makes \(\lceil b_{n+1}^2/b_n\rceil-1=b_{n+2}\), identifying the original nonlinear sequence with the linear-recurrence sequence and hence yielding the stated generating function.

full_proof.text:
Let \((a_n)_{n\ge 0}\) denote the sequence given by the original definition. Thus
\[
a_0=4,\qquad a_1=16,
\]
and, for every \(n\ge 0\),
\[
a_{n+2}=\left\lceil \frac{a_{n+1}^2}{a_n}\right\rceil-1.
\tag{1}
\]
For positive terms this is equivalent to the extremal ratio formulation: an integer \(m\) satisfies
\[
\frac{m}{a_{n+1}}<\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}
\]
if and only if \(m<a_{n+1}^2/a_n\), and the greatest integer strictly smaller than a real number \(x\) is \(\lceil x\rceil-1\).

We prove that \((a_n)\) is the sequence determined by
\[
b_0=4,\qquad b_1=16,\qquad b_2=63,
\tag{2}
\]
and
\[
b_{n+3}=4b_{n+2}-b_n\qquad(n\ge 0).
\tag{3}
\]
The main point is to prove that the ceiling in (1) always produces the right-hand side candidate. For that purpose we need both growth estimates for \(b_n\) and precise control of the remainder when \(b_{n+1}^2\) is divided by \(b_n\).

First, all the \(b_n\) are positive and grow by at least a factor of two:
\[
0<b_n,\qquad 2b_n\le b_{n+1}\qquad(n\ge 0).
\tag{4}
\]
We prove these two assertions simultaneously by strong induction. The first few candidate terms are
\[
b_0=4,\quad b_1=16,\quad b_2=63,\quad b_3=4\cdot63-4=248.
\]
Consequently the claims for \(n=0,1,2\) follow from
\[
8\le16,\qquad32\le63,\qquad126\le248.
\]
Now suppose that the claims with lower indices are known and consider index \(k+3\). The induction assertion at index \(k+2\) gives
\[
0<b_{k+2},\qquad 2b_{k+2}\le b_{k+3},
\]
so in particular \(b_{k+3}>0\). To establish the required growth inequality from \(b_{k+3}\) to \(b_{k+4}\), use
\[
b_{k+4}=4b_{k+3}-b_{k+1}.
\]
The preceding growth inequalities imply
\[
2b_{k+1}\le b_{k+2},\qquad 2b_{k+2}\le b_{k+3},
\]
and hence certainly \(b_{k+1}\le2b_{k+3}\). It follows that
\[
b_{k+4}=4b_{k+3}-b_{k+1}\ge2b_{k+3}.
\]
This completes the induction and proves (4). In particular, every subtraction in (3) has a nonnegative result. We may therefore also write the recurrence in the subtraction-free form
\[
b_{n+3}+b_n=4b_{n+2}.
\tag{5}
\]

We now introduce an auxiliary sequence \((r_n)_{n\ge0}\), defined by
\[
r_0=4,\qquad r_1=1,\qquad r_2=16,
\tag{6}
\]
and
\[
r_{n+3}=4r_{n+1}+r_n\qquad(n\ge0).
\tag{7}
\]
We will prove two facts about these numbers:
\[
0<r_n\le b_n
\tag{8}
\]
and
\[
b_{n+1}^2=b_n b_{n+2}+r_n.
\tag{9}
\]
Thus \(r_n\) will be exactly the positive remainder, in a slightly generalized sense that permits \(r_n=b_n\), between the square \(b_{n+1}^2\) and the multiple \(b_n b_{n+2}\).

We first prove (8) by strong induction. At indices \(0,1,2\), it is immediate from
\[
0<4\le4,\qquad0<1\le16,\qquad0<16\le63.
\]
For the induction step, suppose the bounds are known at indices \(k\) and \(k+1\). From (7),
\[
r_{k+3}=4r_{k+1}+r_k>0.
\]
Moreover,
\[
r_{k+3}\le4b_{k+1}+b_k.
\tag{10}
\]
By the growth bounds (4),
\[
2b_k\le b_{k+1},\qquad 2b_{k+1}\le b_{k+2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
4b_{k+1}+2b_k\le5b_{k+1}\le8b_{k+1}\le4b_{k+2}.
\]
Rearranging this gives
\[
4b_{k+1}+b_k\le4b_{k+2}-b_k=b_{k+3}.
\]
Together with (10), this proves \(r_{k+3}\le b_{k+3}\), completing the proof of (8).

We next establish the exact identity (9), again by strong induction. The first three cases are direct calculations. Namely,
\[
16^2=256=4\cdot63+4,
\]
\[
63^2=3969=16\cdot248+1,
\]
and, since
\[
b_4=4b_3-b_1=4\cdot248-16=976,
\]
we have
\[
248^2=61504=63\cdot976+16.
\]
These are precisely (9) for \(n=0,1,2\).

For the induction step, assume (9) at indices \(k\) and \(k+1\). To make the algebra transparent, put
\[
A=b_k,\quad B=b_{k+1},\quad C=b_{k+2},\quad D=b_{k+3},\quad E=b_{k+4},\quad F=b_{k+5}.
\]
The recurrence gives
\[
D+A=4C,\qquad E+B=4D,\qquad F+C=4E.
\tag{11}
\]
The two induction hypotheses are
\[
B^2=AC+r_k,
\qquad
C^2=BD+r_{k+1}.
\tag{12}
\]
Using (11), we compute
\[
\begin{aligned}
E^2-DF
 &=E^2-D(4E-C)\\
 &=E(E-4D)+DC\\
 &=-BE+DC\\
 &=-B(4D-B)+DC\\
 &=DC-4BD+B^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(D+A=4C\), multiplication by \(C\) gives
\[
DC=4C^2-AC.
\]
Consequently, using (12),
\[
\begin{aligned}
E^2-DF
 &=4C^2-AC-4BD+B^2\\
 &=4(C^2-BD)+(B^2-AC)\\
 &=4r_{k+1}+r_k\\
 &=r_{k+3}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\[
b_{k+4}^2=b_{k+3}b_{k+5}+r_{k+3},
\]
which is (9) at index \(k+3\). The induction is complete.

We now use (8) and (9) to show that the nonlinear original sequence \((a_n)\) coincides with the linear-recurrence candidate \((b_n)\). We proceed by strong induction on the index. At indices \(0\) and \(1\), the equality follows from the common initial values \(4,16\).

Suppose now that equality has already been proved through the two indices needed to calculate \(a_{k+2}\), namely
\[
a_k=b_k,
\qquad
a_{k+1}=b_{k+1}.
\]
By (9),
\[
b_{k+1}^2=b_kb_{k+2}+r_k,
\tag{13}
\]
and by (8),
\[
0<r_k\le b_k.
\tag{14}
\]
Because \(b_k>0\), division of (13) by \(b_k\) yields
\[
\frac{b_{k+1}^2}{b_k}=b_{k+2}+\frac{r_k}{b_k},
\]
where
\[
0<\frac{r_k}{b_k}\le1.
\]
It follows that
\[
\left\lceil\frac{b_{k+1}^2}{b_k}\right\rceil=b_{k+2}+1.
\tag{15}
\]
This remains true in the endpoint case \(r_k=b_k\): then the quotient is exactly \(b_{k+2}+1\). In all other cases it lies strictly between \(b_{k+2}\) and \(b_{k+2}+1\).

Substituting the induction hypotheses into the original recurrence (1), and then using (15), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{k+2}
 &=\left\lceil\frac{a_{k+1}^2}{a_k}\right\rceil-1\\
 &=\left\lceil\frac{b_{k+1}^2}{b_k}\right\rceil-1\\
 &=b_{k+2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus strong induction proves
\[
a_n=b_n\qquad\text{for every }n\ge0.
\tag{16}
\]
In particular, the original sequence begins
\[
4,16,63,248,976,3841,\ldots,
\]
since
\[
b_3=4\cdot63-4=248,
\quad b_4=4\cdot248-16=976,
\quad b_5=4\cdot976-63=3841.
\]

Combining (16) with the defining recurrence (3) for \(b_n\), we obtain the desired linear recurrence for the original sequence:
\[
a_0=4,
\qquad a_1=16,
\qquad a_2=63,
\]
and, for every \(n\ge3\),
\[
a_n=4a_{n-1}-a_{n-3}.
\tag{17}
\]

It remains to translate (17) into the claimed generating function. Let
\[
G(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}a_nx^n.
\]
This may be viewed purely as a formal power series. The coefficient of \(x^n\) in
\[
(1-4x+x^3)G(x)
\]
is \(a_n-4a_{n-1}+a_{n-3}\), with terms of negative index omitted. For \(n\ge3\), this coefficient is zero by (17). The first three coefficients are
\[
a_0=4,
\]
\[
a_1-4a_0=16-16=0,
\]
and
\[
a_2-4a_1=63-64=-1.
\]
Therefore
\[
(1-4x+x^3)G(x)=4-x^2,
\]
and hence
\[
\boxed{G(x)=\frac{4-x^2}{1-4x+x^3}}.
\]
This proves the conjectured generating function for the original-definition variant.
